prompt.context: Montoya Soup Co. is a Business Unit of Izzy's Healthy Foods. In F14, Montoya grew revenue and increased the contribution margins on their Traditional and Light Soups. However, a spike in fixed costs caused a dip in profitability. To offset this in F15, they launched a line of premium soups in an attempt to increase volume and generate economies of scale. Though they felt the new launch was a success, their profitability dropped again in F15.
prompt.question: They have hired you to diagnose the problem and propose a solution for F16.

clarifying_info.q: What product lines does Montoya Soup Co. have?
clarifying_info.a: Traditional, Light, and Premium are the only product lines in Montoya Soup Co.'s product portfolio.

clarifying_info.q: How does Montoya sell its products?
clarifying_info.a: Montoya sells cases to buyers at grocery retailers who mark up the units inside to sell to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: What drove revenue growth in F15?
clarifying_info.a: Growth was driven by the premium line. There was some cannibalization of traditional and light lines.

clarifying_info.q: Did input prices or formulations change for Traditional and Light in F15?
clarifying_info.a: Input prices are the same as F14 for the traditional and light lines. No additional wastage. No change in formulation.

clarifying_info.q: What happened to fixed costs in F15?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs were flat at $1.3bn in F15.

exhibits.title: Performance metrics
exhibits.shows: Line chart and table showing year-over-year percentage changes and absolute values for Sales Volume, Sales Revenue, Contribution Margin, and Gross Margin from F10 to F15

exhibits.title: Product lines
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart of variable input costs per case for Traditional, Light, and Premium products; table of wholesale prices and volumes in F14 and F15; and a quote from management about the premium launch rationale

exhibits.title: Demand analysis
exhibits.shows: Table comparing demand and cannibalization effects at the current premium price vs. a raised price; management quotes describing two cost-reduction scenarios (packaging change and meat/vegetable reduction)

data.Packaging change scenario: Would gain $3 margin per case, decrease demand by 20%, spike Traditional cannibalization to 75%
data.Meat and vegetable reduction scenario: Would gain $3 margin per case; consumers should not notice the difference in the short run

exhibits.title: Stakeholder input
exhibits.shows: Customer (grocery retailer) feedback and consumer focus group excerpts about the premium launch

Customer feedback highlights: Premium brought a new consumer to the shelf-stable soup category
Planning to give more shelf space to Montoya in F16 after successful premium launch
High repeat purchase rate among trial buyers
Consumer focus group highlights: Consumer switched from Traditional to Premium due to BPA-free carton packaging
Consumer values higher meat and vegetable content as a bargain

framework: Revenue: analyze volume trends, price trends, and product mix (cannibalization across Traditional, Light, Premium)
Costs: separate fixed vs. variable; fixed were flat in F15 so focus on variable costs
Product Mix: assess contribution margin per product line to identify margin dilution
Pricing strategy: evaluate elasticity and cannibalization trade-offs to optimize portfolio profitability

questions.prompt: What trends do you see with regard to top-line growth from Exhibit A?
questions.guidance: Revenue grew significantly in F15 (from $3,680M to $4,200M), much faster than in any prior year. Sales volume also increased (140M to 155M cases). However, revenue outpaced volume growth, meaning average price per case rose. Despite revenue growth, Contribution Margin was essentially flat ($1,360M in F14 vs. $1,356M in F15) and Gross Margin declined ($60.0M to $56.0M). The candidate should infer that variable costs must have increased to explain flat contribution margin on higher revenue.

questions.prompt: Fixed costs were flat. What happened with variable costs, and how do you know?
questions.guidance: Fixed Costs = Contribution Margin - Gross Margin. In F14: $1,360M - $60.0M = $1,300M. In F15: $1,356M - $56.0M = $1,300M. Fixed costs confirmed flat at $1.3bn. Since revenue rose but contribution margin was flat, variable cost per case (or total variable costs) must have increased. The driver is a product mix shift toward Premium, which has a lower contribution margin than Traditional and Light, AND cannibalizes the higher-margin lines.

math.setup: Gross Margin = Contribution Margin - Fixed Costs. Fixed Costs = CM - GM.
steps: Fixed costs are flat; variable cost mix must be the issue
math.answer: Fixed costs flat at $1.3bn; variable cost mix shifted due to premium line

questions.prompt: Calculate the contribution margin per case for each product line using Exhibit B.
questions.guidance: Traditional: Price $28 - variable costs ($1+$7+$3+$1+$4+$1 = $17 implied from bar chart reading $18 total... the casebook states $10 contribution margin on Traditional). Light: Price $24 - variable costs = $10 contribution margin. Premium: Price $30 - variable costs ($1+$8+$6+$1+$7+$1 = $24) = $6 contribution margin. The key insight is that Premium has a $6/case margin vs. $10/case for Traditional and Light.

math.setup: Contribution Margin per case = Wholesale Price - Sum of Variable Costs per case

questions.prompt: Calculate net profit generated by the Premium line last year (F15), accounting for cannibalization of Traditional and Light.
questions.guidance: Net profit from Premium = Premium profit - Traditional profit lost from cannibalization - Light profit lost from cannibalization. Premium: 40M cases x $6 = $240M profit. Traditional cannibalized: 50% of 40M = 20M cases x $10 = $200M lost. Light cannibalized: 12.5% of 40M = 5M cases x $10 = $50M lost. Net = $240M - $200M - $50M = -$10M. The Premium launch actually destroyed $10M of profit.

math.setup: Net Profit = (Premium volume x Premium margin) - (Trad cannibalization x Trad margin) - (Light cannibalization x Light margin)
math.answer: -$10M; the Premium line destroyed value in F15

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit C, evaluate three options to fix profitability: (1) change packaging (cans), (2) reduce meat and vegetables, (3) raise price to $33. Calculate net profit from Premium under each scenario.
questions.guidance: Option 1 - Change packaging: margin becomes $9, demand drops 20% to 32M cases, Traditional cannibalization spikes to 75% (24M cases). Net = (32x$9) - (24x$10) - (5x$10) = $288 - $240 - $50 = -$2M. Still negative and harms brand. Option 2 - Reduce meat/veg: margin becomes $9, demand stays at 40M, cannibalization unchanged. Net = (40x$9) - (20x$10) - (5x$10) = $360 - $200 - $50 = $110M. Profitable but erodes quality/brand long-term. Option 3 - Raise price to $33: margin becomes $9 ($33-$24), demand drops to 20M, Traditional cannibalization drops to 10% (2M cases), Light cannibalization = 0%. Net = (20x$9) - (2x$10) - (0x$10) = $180 - $20 - $0 = $160M. Best outcome and preserves quality.

math.setup: Net Profit = (Premium vol x new margin) - (Trad cannib vol x $10) - (Light cannib vol x $10)
steps: Option 1 (change packaging to can): margin=$9, vol=32M, Trad cannib=75%x32M=24M, Light cannib=5M => $288-$240-$50=-$2M
Option 2 (reduce meat/veg): margin=$9, vol=40M, Trad cannib=50%x40M=20M, Light cannib=5M => $360-$200-$50=$110M
Option 3 (raise price to $33): margin=$9, vol=20M, Trad cannib=10%x20M=2M, Light cannib=0M => $180-$20-$0=$160M
math.answer: Option 1: -$2M; Option 2: $110M; Option 3: $160M — raise price to $33 is the optimal strategy

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit D tell us about the long-run viability of cost-reduction options vs. price increase?
questions.guidance: Retailers are enthusiastic about the Premium line and plan to give more shelf space in F16. Consumers value the carton packaging (BPA-free) and higher meat/vegetable content. Reducing quality (Option 2) would undermine the value proposition and erode brand equity in the long run. Raising prices (Option 3) is the only option that maintains quality, and consumer data supports a premium willingness-to-pay.

brainstorming.prompt: What could have driven up Montoya's variable costs in F15?

categories.name: Input price changes
ideas: Commodity price increases for meat, vegetables, or packaging materials

categories.name: Formulation or recipe changes
ideas: Higher meat and vegetable content in Premium vs. Traditional
More expensive packaging format (carton vs. can) for Premium line

categories.name: Product mix shift
ideas: Cannibalization of higher-margin Traditional and Light by lower-margin Premium
Larger share of total volume coming from Premium with $6 margin vs. $10 for other lines

categories.name: Operational inefficiencies
ideas: Increased manufacturing waste during new Premium line ramp-up
Lower economies of scale on new production line initially

categories.name: Distribution/logistics
ideas: Higher shipping cost per case for carton packaging vs. cans
New distribution channels required for premium product

recommendation: Increase the price of the Premium line from $30 to $33 per case
At $33, net profit from Premium would increase to $160M (vs. -$10M at $30), as cannibalization of Traditional drops from 50% to 10% and volume decline is offset by higher margin
Do not reduce meat/vegetable content or switch to can packaging — these options damage the brand equity and quality proposition that drives consumer loyalty and retailer support
risks: Pricing measures did not consider competitive response — a competitor could enter the premium soup space at a lower price point and force Montoya out of the category
Raising prices could upset some grocery buyers and result in lost shelf distribution
Some price-sensitive consumers who switched from Traditional for the 'bargain' may return to Traditional or switch to competitors
Opportunity cost: a long-term strategy of phasing out Traditional/Light and scaling Premium at current price could be more valuable
next_steps: Perform due diligence on long-term consumer preference forecasts and competitive dynamics in the premium soup segment
Launch an advertising campaign to justify higher prices and defend against potential competitive entry
Explore reducing high fixed costs ($1.3bn) to build resilience against price-aggressive competitors or commodity price increases
Monitor cannibalization rates closely after price increase to validate elasticity assumptions
